# How Do Reviews of Phantom Blade Zero Compare Now with the Launch Period?

Reviews for **Phantom Blade Zero** remain overwhelmingly positive, with recent English reviews showing 3.7% negative and Simplified Chinese showing 3.0% negative between November 5 and November 8, 2026 [R7][R8], compared to 5.3% negative for English and 3.3% negative for Simplified Chinese during the launch window of October 29 to November 4, 2026 [R9][R10]. This slight positive trend followed the release of Patch 1.0302256 on November 4, 2026, which addressed critical technical bugs like shader compilation stutters and control mapping issues [R6]. While early complaints heavily criticized performance drops and unresponsive controls [R54][R68], recent criticisms have shifted to minor environmental collision issues [R48], while both periods saw praise for the game's responsive combat, beautiful art direction, and music [R11][R15][R21].

### Timeline

*   **October 28, 2026**: **Phantom Blade Zero** is released on Windows by S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing for $59.99 [R3]. S-GAME publishes the developer announcement titled "Reason and Madness" reflecting on franchise history [R5].
*   **October 29 – November 4, 2026**: Launch review period [R9][R10]. In sampled reviews, English reviewers submit 284 positive and 16 negative reviews, while Simplified Chinese reviewers submit 290 positive and 10 negative reviews [R9][R10].
*   **November 4, 2026**: S-GAME releases patch version 1.0302256, adding sound options, remapping for keyboard and controller, easing boss grab attacks on Wayfarer and Pathbreaker difficulties, and optimization improvements for PC shaders [R6].
*   **November 5 – November 8, 2026**: Recent review period [R7][R8]. Sampled English reviews contain 289 positive and 11 negative reviews, while Simplified Chinese reviews contain 291 positive and 9 negative reviews [R7][R8].
*   **November 8, 2026**: The game records a current player count of 349043 on Steam [R4].

### What players say

During the recent period, 96.3% of sampled English reviews and 97.0% of Simplified Chinese reviews were positive, maintaining the strong positive momentum from the launch period [R7][R8][R9].

#### Praise
Positive reviewers continuously praise **Phantom Blade Zero** for its butter-smooth, highly responsive combat system, outstanding fluid animations, and satisfying weapon diversity [R11][R15][R17]. Players also express appreciation for the game's engaging wuxia atmospheric music, great art direction, and Chinese voice acting [R15][R17][R18]. At launch, some players specifically praised the design choice of non-respawning enemies, though this was divisive as others felt it left maps feeling empty [R29][R70].
*   "BEST ACTION GAME I'VE EXPERIENCED IN THE RECENT YEARS." (57.8 hours played) [R11]
*   "Every weapon feels so different and unique while all feeling extremely satisfying to try out with the exclusive animations for them all." (59.8 hours played) [R15]

#### Criticism
Negative feedback has evolved since launch. In the launch window, players complained about severe shader compilation stutters, delayed texture loading, frame drops, frequent crashes, and AMD GPU glitches [R54][R56][R62]. They also criticized key remapping bugs and unresponsive dodge inputs [R55][R68]. Following the November 4 patch [R6], recent complaints highlight other optimization issues on GTX 50s [R46] and collision bugs where players get stuck on small ledges or rocks [R48]. Others complain about invisible walls [R43] or dismiss the combat across both windows as repetitive button-mashing or heavily scripted [R42][R52][R53].
*   "I should not be getting stuck on little ledges, of walk ways, rocks, pieces of wood, etc." (25.3 hours played) [R48]

### What the data can't answer

*   The data cannot track historical player count peaks or averages for **Phantom Blade Zero** from its launch on October 29 through November 8, 2026.
*   The total number of owners cannot be verified because SteamSpy's owner estimate is out of date and contradicts the active player count [R4].
*   There is no console data available, as the sources only cover Steam and Windows platforms [R3][R4].
*   Steam reviews only represent players who chose to post reviews.
*   Developer motivations are only known as stated in official announcements [R5].

R5.text:
Reason and Madness

Twenty years ago, while I was still a student, I completed my first indie game, Rainblood: Town of Death. It was a hobby project made with RPG Maker. With the limited skills I had at the time, I built the fantasy world I had imagined: the Phantom World, rooted in traditional Chinese wuxia but infused with elements such as body modification, parallel worlds, and more.

Back then, I had no idea where my life or career would lead. Making games had simply been a source of comfort while I studied abroad, but before I knew it, it had become one of the most important parts of my life.

More than three years ago, when we brought our first, still rather rough trailer for Phantom Blade Zero to a PlayStation Showcase, we probably looked like a new studio being a little too bold, putting an unfinished game out for the whole world to judge. Phantom Blade was simply another original IP, its world, characters, and story entirely unfamiliar to most people.

But that moment marked the beginning of an extraordinary journey.

We cancelled our other projects in development and kept expanding the scale of production, refining every detail, and bringing together all the technology, expertise, resources, and support we could. Thousands of hours of motion capture. Visits to towns and mountain villages across China to scan them in 3D. Lion dance choreography guided by masters from Guangdong, sword formations guided by sword masters from Mount Emei, and hand-to-hand techniques guided by monks from the Shaolin Temple. We also assembled a dedicated team of professional martial arts performers for motion capture, led by action director Yang Liu. With guidance from our hero, Donnie Yen, the team created countless attacks, defensive moves, dodges, combos, and executions for the game.

You may have already seen plenty of reviews of Phantom Blade Zero, but if you’d rather avoid spoilers, you can always experience the game for yourself. Once you start playing, much of it will feel natural, simple, and familiar. We have taken those familiar elements, reimagined them, and brought them together into something new.

Over the past few years, we have taken a close look at many of the conventions that action RPGs and action games have long treated as unwritten rules. We have asked ourselves what players want most, and how to bring those elements together to achieve our goal: a game that everyone who loves wuxia and spectacular action can enjoy. After all, this is a game. We want as many people as possible to have fun, unwind, and enjoy the experience, while offering an extra rush of adrenaline to those who seek a challenge.

Throughout development, we have spoken with countless players at shows and hands-on events, from Beijing and Shanghai to Los Angeles and São Paulo. Those conversations helped us better understand what players want, and we have tried to bring that same care to even the smallest details.

For example, our audio settings include an option to adjust the tone of clashing blades, so you can tailor how each clash sounds and feels. On PS5, we offer three different button layouts, with more flexible remapping options on PC. We have also adapted the game for all major screen aspect ratios, including 16:9 monitors and TVs, 16:10 laptops and handhelds, and ultrawide displays with aspect ratios beyond 3:1.

But making games is not always a rational pursuit. Sometimes, it is passion and a little madness that give a game its richest flavor. Several of our key battles were created by a few young teammates in their twenties. Our Art Director, Michael Chang, single-handedly drew the concept art for every character and most of our environments. And then there is our Music Director, Caisheng Bo, who has never been one to hold back. He created more than ten hours of music almost entirely by himself. Aside from a few special instruments and vocal performances, he handled everything, including composition, performance, and mixing. He also guided the implementation of the music in the game, including playback, volume control, and more.

After years of development, I feel that technology and experience have become the baseline, almost a given at this point. What I find myself paying more attention to now is the mindset of the people behind the game. Beyond skill and experience, is there also a certain madness, a certain obsession? Somewhere along the way, as we kept making a wuxia game, it started to feel like we ourselves were becoming the kind of people you would find in a wuxia story.

Over the past few years, one thing I often said to the team was, “Today, I have a suffocating decision to announce.” That usually meant taking apart something everyone had already carefully built and polished, then rebuilding it, or even abandoning it altogether. It meant a great deal of rework, and sometimes letting go of content that had already taken an enormous amount of time and effort. I am deeply grateful to the team for their understanding and support. We did it. We have poured all our thought and creativity into this game.

Phantom Blade Zero exists to make you feel powerful and incredibly cool. No matter what enemy stands before you, you will defeat them in the end. That feeling has to come from more than simply telling you how strong you are. It has to come through every slash of your blade, every block, every dodge, and every dazzling execution shaped by the game’s brutal aesthetic. Your enemies are powerful so that your own strength can feel even greater. Even the story’s darkness, its touch of tragedy, and the countdown of sixty-six days left to live serve that same purpose: to take that sense of strength beyond what you can do in battle and make it something you feel within yourself.

And now, with all our hearts, we invite you to experience Phantom Blade Zero.

 

Its roots lie in the indie game I created during my student years, at a time of hardship and uncertainty. But it also holds everything we have been able to give.

 

This is a game of immense scale, made with all the passion in our hearts. It is a gift from a small group of gamers who just happen to be developers, to every gamer who shares our love for gaming.

 

See you in the Phantom World!

The Duality of Phantom Blade Zero: Overrated or Exactly What You're Looking For

This is the first time I've felt the need to write a review of a game, mainly because I want to save some people from potentially making a mistake. So let me explain that somewhat confusing title.

First of all, this game looks absolutely beautiful. The art direction is fantastic, same as the music and simply walking around and exploring the world is genuinely enjoyable. A lot of that comes down to how good the movement looks and feels, with your character effortlessly running, dodging, and jumping through the environment. The lovingly crafted world only adds to that impression. The same goes for the combat: at first glance, it looks incredibly cool and flashy.

However, the more time you spend with the game, and the more you approach its mechanics and story expecting a certain level of depth, the more obvious it becomes that this is a fairly average experience at its core.

It starts with the combat. The flashy first impression wears off a little once you want to deep-dive into it which especially shows in the blocking system. At some point you'll realize that you don't even have to time your blocks properly. You can simply hold down the block button, and as long as you regularly switch weapons to keep your Sha-Chi meter filled, you basically won't take any damage which culminates in you just holding block even while attacking to be invulnerable.

Of course, enemies also have red and blue attacks that you can't just block and instead have to respond to with a perfectly timed parry or dodge. But when you spend most of the fight doing nothing other than holding block, occasionally switching weapons to have enough Sha-Chi, and watching out for those red and blue attacks, it's honestly pretty difficult to mess up the timing.

Successfully parrying or dodging these attacks damages the enemy's posture, eventually giving you a short window to hit them with light or heavy attacks. Outside of those windows, however, there's barely any reason to attack at all, since many of the later enemies will either parry pretty much everything or simply be invulnerable until you've broken their posture.

Now this is the most important part of my problem with this game: As a result, what initially looks like a very dynamic combat system gradually turns into a rather mindless waiting game. You wait for the right attacks, dodge or parry them, break the enemy's posture, and then spend the next 10 seconds mashing the same button over and over again until the enemy becomes untouchable again. I think there could be a pretty interesting combat system but the game just does not let me use it. Also: This pattern repeats an absurd number of times on Hellwalker difficulty, since the bosses are a somewhat damage spongy until, after a while, the difficulty starts to feel somewhat artificial, because the mechanics aren't particularly demanding, but because you're forced to repeat the same simple sequence throughout the whole fight. What underlines this impression is that your character is sometimes practically fighting on his own. You'll find yourself watching these long, elaborate combos that look impressive, while all you're actually doing is repeatedly pressing the same button. This takes away some of the impact and directness of the combat, because what happens on screen doesn't always feel proportional to what you're actually doing.

(Additionally some bosses are so shamelessly copied from other games that it's almost funny. Jing Ye is just Gyoubu Oniwa from Sekiro. But that's not really part of my criticism.)

The story suffers from a similar problem. With its beautiful cutscenes and wonderfully detailed characters, it makes a great first impression. But once you actually start paying attention to the dialogue and try to follow what's happening, so many things feel completely random, absurd, or like they came out of nowhere. At some point, you almost have to stop questioning things to enjoy it.

Even the beautifully designed map becomes rather annoying once you actually try to use it. It's so inaccurate that some markers seem to indicate only the rough general area of whatever you're looking for. I once spent around ten minutes searching for an interaction shown on the map, only to eventually realize it was much farther east and somewhere deep inside the mountain below me.
Eventually, I just started ignoring the map altogether. If a map is going to be unreliable, just don't put it in the game. Let players miss things if they're not paying enough attention while exploring. 

Conclusion: I think Phantom Blade Zero was apparently designed to appeal to a very broad audience which is not necessarily bad. An accessible game can have mechanical depth and a hard game can be mechanically very simple. But this game wants to be accessible while also trying to offer a somewhat challenging and demanding experience here and there. And I don't think it quite manages to balance those two ambitions. Sometimes it just feels a little undecided about what kind of game it wants to be.

With all that said, I really want to emphasize again just how beautiful this game is. The animations, the movement, the huge variety of weapons and their different fighting styles, the fantastically staged boss encounters, and the world itself are all seriously amazing. There's a lot of enjoyment in this game.

But if you're looking for demanding, precise gameplay with a lot of mechanical depth, where your inputs feel deliberate and every action matters, I think there's a good chance you'll end up somewhat disappointed.

(BTW: I'm not even saying that Phantom Blade Zero necessarily pretends to be an extremely deep or demanding Soulslike - the devs even said that this is not a Soulslike. It's just that, judging by its presentation and the sheer number of mechanics it introduces, you could easily get the impression that there's much more depth beneath the surface than there actually is.)

If, on the other hand, you're looking for a beautiful hack-and-slash game to enjoy looking like a character from "House Of Flying Daggers" while fighting your way through an amazing world, this might genuinely be your game of the year.

TL;DR: The aesthetics, animations, and world design are S-tier. But if you're expecting precise, deliberate combat with a high skill ceiling, you might be disappointed. Despite how impressive everything looks, many of the combos require very little input, defensive mechanics are surprisingly forgiving, and boss fights often boil down to waiting for specific attacks before getting another opportunity to deal damage. The game is much more about spectacle than mechanical depth. Whether that's a problem depends entirely on what you're looking for.

I had been genuinely excited for this game from the second it was announced, and to keep it short and sweet, it did not come close to my expectations.

Overall, graphically it is above average. The world is very pretty, but the effects definitely break that immersion—the quality of things like blood splatter and water animation just seems so much lower than the environment.

Narratively, I have not been able to get drawn into it. That’s not really important for this kind of game, but I couldn’t care less about any of the dialogue or cutscenes, which is a bit disappointing.

Now to the important part: combat. The combat in this game, flashy as it may be, is just that. Perfect Block and Parry windows are terrible outside of the blue and red flashes. Combat is essentially reduced to just holding block while attacking and weapon swapping if you don’t want to be overly punished by artificial difficulty.

And that is my BIGGEST problem with the combat: artificial difficulty in boss fights. Whether it be attacks blending in with the environment, using one animation to block another (causing you to miss your cues or straight-up hide them), stirring up the environment to block your vision, or spamming low-visibility attacks while you’re in the middle of handling the last one without a large enough window to read it—the real enemy is not being able to actually see what is going on.

Obviously, I am still early on with only 10 hours in, but if the trend of boss fights continues to be riddled with vision obstruction, artificial difficulty, and overly flashy animations instead of actual engaging combat, then I will not be completing this game. I had been playing on Hellwalker, but apparently that difficulty allows enemies to adapt to your play and perform feints and combo cancellations, along with other differences that punish the player for learning the boss itself.

If my opinion changes, I will update my review. I will be proceeding on Pathfinder difficulty from here on.

For me, Phantom Blade was a wishlist game since it was announced. While the game has a fun element to it, the combat can be reduced to a button mashing spam fest that leaves a lot of disappointment. I held off on getting this due to some of the feedback it was getting, and while I think the feedback was a little unfair, I do believe the game is bit overhyped. Games like this show that the unwashed masses of the gaming market are more interested in flashy animations, cinematics, and other forms of feedback they aren't really in control of, and therefore plays it for them in some respects. To put it more bluntly, gamers today are more impressed with games that make you feel more skilled than you really are rather than becoming better at the game through failure and actually getting better. 

To start, the animations are so plentiful that it is often hard to tell when the game is playing itself or if you are. This just left me bitter at times. Even on hellwalker, the game didn't feel as challenging as I thought it would. Instead, after rolling through a couple of mini-bosses and bosses, the challenge quickly became more artificial. When am I actually playing? Yes, there's moves sets that the game controls, not you. But, during blocks sequences, this also happens, so much so that on many occasions if you miss the first series of an enemy attack, there is no way to catch up to block any additional attacks in that series. Because you're stuck in an enemy animation feeback that has to play out. No way to heal during this, no way to escape, no way to block effectively. This isn't always the case though. Sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. And that's frustrating. Am I going to get stuck in this particular attack pattern if I don't start it off perfectly? Or, can I be less than perfect, and get back on track. Hard to say, really. Each boss is different so far. 

On a further note, the block timing in this game is just plain bad. What feels like a naturally timed block isn't, and you're stuck testing this out over and over again. To the point where you're really just frustratingly spamming. I've seen many people admitting they're just holding the block button down while attacking to mitigate incoming damage. 

This leads to another issue. People obviously aren't always capable seeing, or even knowing, when to block or parry, or when to dodge. They're just holding block for dear life, or spamming dodge, and letting luck take the wheel. 

A combat system built on these issues is not good. I'm sorry. Flashy animations aren't going to save it. 

The story isn't anything interesting. It's also weighed down by ill-defined metaphysical concepts that aren't really explained well through dialogue, and while there may be more explanations in the text, the game operates on the principle that everything is so fast all the time, that slowing down to read doesn't make sense. I'm not much of a lore guy myself, so that doesn't help either. It also doesn't help this a Chinese game, and Chinese games are often hyper-cheesy with their dialogue and stories. 

There is fun to be had here. It's a button mashing hack and slash on steroids with flashy animations and cinematics. And if you're here to mindlessly swing for the fences while being made feel god-like through animations that happen often in your fights, while look no further. This game is for you. For me, it's a bit of a disappointment and nothing to really write home about so far. I will finish it but I have nothing extremely positive to say about it.

R53.text:
I wish Steam had a "Meh" option, because that's exactly where I land on this one.

This game was sold on the promise of Sekiro-level combat, and I'm just not seeing it. What we actually got feels more like an anime dressed up as a game.

Boss encounters are essentially heavily scripted action movies. You hold block, wait for the flashy visual cue, hit the corresponding bumper, and get a few seconds to actually attack the boss. Rinse and repeat.

Eventually, you realize you're not really fighting the boss. You're **waiting for the boss to give you permission to play the game.** Four seconds of actual combat, followed by another round of waiting for the next flashy, choreographed sequence.

And that's my biggest disappointment. The supposedly deep, expressive combat system only really gets room to breathe against trash mobs, which die far too quickly for any of that depth to matter. The boss fights, where that combat should truly shine, are instead dominated by scripted spectacle.

Now, I'll absolutely give the game credit where it's due. It looks sick as hell. The animations, presentation, and sheer spectacle are genuinely impressive. But looking incredible and being engaging to actually play are two very different things.

I also think some game journalists need to get better at recognizing when they're being sold a carefully curated experience rather than critically evaluating the game underneath all that spectacle. A stunning boss animation isn't automatically good combat design.

There's a genuinely interesting combat system buried in here. I just wish the game would get out of its own way and let me use it.

R57.text:
FYI i have been playing this game on highest difficulty you can choose on first run. This game is okay at best IMO. The move sets are cool but they are so not practical in this game. No matter what you do, once you deplete your "turn", the enemies WILL take their turns to attack you even when you are continuing your combos. Doesn't matter if you are faster or better. Once you use your turn, the enemy's gotta have its' turn to attack you no matter what. So you are forced to have this flow of turns between you and the enemy through out the whole battle. BTW the combo you can do is basically press light attacks 1 to 5  times and maybe add few strong attacks at the end. That's pretty much all you can do. The combo animations are cool but you will soon realize that the "combos" are shallow as hell. Not satisfying when hitting enemies since it feels so light even when you land the attacks.

I can see that the devs tried hard to deviate from usual souls like games and action games but this turned out to be so shallow on both criteria. Is it more satisfying and more stylish than DMC 5? No. Is it more satisfying than Elden ring when you beat the boss? No. 

It's definitely not a bad game at all but I am not sure if it lives up to the hype that everyone has built up so far.

R58.text:
This is just my opinion, and I want to share it, so people who are soulslike fans like me, can see what I think of this game, with a mindset like that.

The selling point of this game is supposed to be the visuals and combat, so I will start with those.

Visually the game looks amazing, there is no point arguing. Combat is flashy, the environment is beautiful.

The combat itself is the real problem for me. I understand the target audience is the casual players, who do not want to get good. But to have a combat loop, where you essentially spam the same button, and the game plays itself is a bit too casual for me. If to pull out a combo for you is to spam the same button, then you will enjoy this combat system. This in itself would not be a problem, if the core of the combat would be deep, but in reality, as long as you confidently spam attacks and parries, you will do just fine 99% of the time. Therefor the combat has no depths, it plays itself. Now there are people who say it is fun, and that is good. I just want to warn people the combat is essentially spam the buttons, and if you do not enjoy to see the same animations over and over again, while you spam the same buttons, then avoid this game. I personally did not enjoy it, and after 15 hours I have had enough. Just do not hope it will get better, because it will not.
Now note that I got halfway through the 4th world, and I saw some okay bosses, but majority of the times, bosses are HP sponges, where you continously have to spam without any brain activity. As I said there are exceptions, but that is quite rare considering how much you have to fight in this game. Some people will say parrying makes the combat not braindead, but I succeded in the hardest difficulty with randomly pressing the parry, because I had no time to learn the timing of the bosses. I just defeated them before it happened.

Exploration sucks. I can not express how disappointed I am. The world visually is so nice, but the invisible walls are everywhere, and you can not find shortcuts other than the very few intended ones. I want to bring up dark souls as an example, how a good exploration works. There the world is connected unexpectedly, and exploration always feel fun because of it. You are free to find funny shortcuts, experiment with the environment. In this game you just go straight, no shortcuts, no exciting experimenting to find ways to explore the world your own way. You are forced in a boring pattern, and you constantly get stuck on random objects. Try to jump down to an area, which you should be able to survive based on height, and the area should be accessible, yet it is instant death. No fun allowed during exploration. 
Also the fact that you unlock different weapons to open up previously unaccessible small areas, is just not fun in this game. This makes it so you are confused. You do not know if you found everything you wanted in the area the first time, or you missed something. This is supposed to be very similar to metroidvania games, which somehow does this idea much better. 
Ultimately exploring became a chore for me.

Music in this game is really good, no complaints about it.

Story is just... please do not expect anything nice. The way it is told is already confusing in itself, randomly jumping around in the timeline, and all I understood is every fking character in this story is an aura farmer, scheming character, and I did not understand their intentions. Everyone is just too smart for you to understand what is going on, because the way dialogues happen, you do not get to understand enough.

Overall the game is not that bad, IF (and this is a big IF), you happen to enjoy flashy braindead combat, and do not care about interesting exploration. The story is not an issue, many games with bad story are fun. So please if you happen to read this, consider my opinions. Consider my viewpoint as a soulslike fan. Otherwise this review might not be for you.

Edit: I got asked in the comments why I hate the combat, and it is similar to Sekiro, so if I love Sekiro, 100% completed the game, then why do I hate this game?

Also why do I not find soulslike combat boring, when it usually is very simple on the surface.

Here is the answer to those:

Soulslike combat have learning curves, you are there to fail and fail until you learn what you need to learn. This results in a satisfaction, pretty much the core of a soulslike. That is also the reason why soulslike players split their community when someone tries to find the most op, easiest to play build, but that is a different topic. But because there are many builds, these type of games have huge replayability values. To have the option to build 100 different builds, and each feel different, is a huge blessing to those, who wants to enjoy the game again. But this only works, if the core of the combat is already good.

Sekiro is not like this either. Sekiro combat seems simple on the surface, yet the combat has a huge learning curve. If you played Sekiro, you will know, each enemy has a visually confirmed rythm. Here visually confirmed is really important to me, because phantom blade zero felt to me like, attacks are coming from nowhere, happening suddenly, which forced me to try to parry everything randomly, and still I succeded the first try majority of the times. Now this made me hate the combat, because there is no satisfaction behind it, other than an eye candy, which gets boring. To me not even the different weapons made this better, because that only resulted way too long combos. Also important to note, that once you deplete a boss's stamina bar, you can do your true combo. This very long true combo takes 20% of the boss's HP. There might be better combos, other than I did, but still the core mechanics are repatativ, and becomes boring, because does not matter what or who you fight, ultimately it will feel the same. Sekiro encounters felt unique, every single of them.

Also while phantom blade zero is not supposed to be soulslike or sekiro like, people still compare them. I think it is because phantom blade zero is trying to imitate those games, yet they say they are not like those game. It's like when palworld took insipration from Pokemon, made it what fanbase wanted from Pokemon for ages, but the difference here is, phantom blade zero made it look worse, copied everything from a soulslike, except it's core, it's heart, which is the most important, what makes soulslike fan. So comparing them should be valid even if they say, phantom blade zero is not meant to be a soulslike.

R59.text:
It feels like two parties masturbating over each other, endlessly trading flashy moves without either side accomplishing anything meaningful.

Victory doesn't feel earned, and defeat doesn't feel instructive. Combat becomes less about skill, strategy, or learning from mistakes and more about participating in an elaborate visual performance. There's plenty of spectacle, but very little substance beneath it.

Every encounter seems designed to impress rather than engage. The result is an exhausting loop of cinematic flourishes, exaggerated animations, and mechanical noise that mistakes visual intensity for meaningful gameplay.

When the dust settles, there's no real satisfaction, no sense of accomplishment, and little incentive to reflect on what went wrong or what went right.

Spectacle slop. All style, no soul.

R60.text:
Phantom Blade Zero is undoubtely an incredibly stylish game, but it compromises heft and depth of gameplay for that style and ultimately fails to impress in a year filled with incredible action games. 

PHZ truly shines in its boss fights. The spectacle of a wuxia style story combined with ridiculously hype moments and music make every boss fight I've played in the 6 odd hours stand out and be memorable, but everything outside of those boss fights, be it the fodder enemies and the traversal, feel like an afterthought. 

Combat also greatly suffers outside of boss fights. There's no heft to the movements, enemies rarely, if ever, react to your moves. Throughout my runtime I kept thinking about Onimusha's fodder enemies and how much better it was to fight them because of its incredible parry and combat system. 

If this game's combat had the same level of polish as Onimusha's does, it would have been a serious game of the year contender. Right now, I cannot recommend it.

R70.text:
I have mixed opinions about this game.

Positives are it looks good, the cutscenes are really good and enjoyable, the combat is fun, storyline is emotional and good. Also once you kill enemies they stay dead (I LOVE THAT) they don’t respawn. 

Negatives are the maps is too big and open meaning its easy to get lost, there is to many side quests along with main stories going on at once, and unlocking new maps without finishing a current one, but its more than one map unlocking at once, so there is so much backtracking its not even funny, there is too much going on, and some boss fights can be extremely hard on the easiest difficulty setting. 

Secondly the heal button (pressing down to heal) you have to be completely still to use that function, and one hit can kill you if you don’t get away fast enough, the heal function should work as soon as you press the button. So that’s frustrating. I have currently unlocked 5-6 maps at this time of making my review about 14hrs in.

So at this stage i am rating this game a 2.5/5. 

It definitely isn’t as good as Onimusha but has similar vibes.

(edit) I now rate it a 1/5 due to lack of effective patches and bug fixes, some parts of the game is just unplayable.
